concept: plain/emphatic consonant pair kept apart (sīn vs ṣād)

concept: sun and moon letters are closed sets that must be memorized, not derived
prompt: A learner keeps mixing up which letters belong to the sun-letter class and which belong to the moon-letter class. Why can this not be worked out from the spelling on the spot?
expected_answer: The sun-letter and moon-letter classes are two closed, fixed lists of letters; nothing in an individual word's spelling reveals which class a given letter belongs to, so membership cannot be derived on the spot from context or from the shape of the letter. The two lists have to be memorized exactly, anchored on the shared articulatory generalization that groups the sun letters together, and then checked against every letter the article precedes.
accepted_variants: sun and moon membership is a closed, memorized list; the spelling of the word gives no clue, so it cannot be worked out on the spot
the two classes are fixed sets learned by rehearsal and an articulatory generalization, not inferred from context each time
forbidden_answers: a letter's spelling reveals on its own whether it is a sun letter or a moon letter
sun and moon membership can be guessed from context each time
the sun-letter list changes depending on the word
required_reasoning: sun and moon classes identified as closed fixed sets
membership identified as not derivable from spelling
memorization anchored on the articulatory generalization

concept: before a sun letter the lām is orthographic only
prompt: A learner pronounces the article's lām even when it precedes a sun letter, reading the written lām as if it were always audible. What decides whether the lām is pronounced?
expected_answer: Whether the article's lām is pronounced is decided by the class of the letter that follows it, not by the fact that a lām is written: before a sun letter the lām is orthographic only, present in the spelling but silent, with its material realized instead as the gemination of the following consonant; before a moon letter the lām stays audible. Pronouncing the lām before a sun letter produces a form no fluent speaker actually uses.
accepted_variants: the following letter's class decides pronunciation: before a sun letter the written lām is silent and its material shows up as gemination instead; before a moon letter it stays audible
the lām before a sun letter is orthographic only, not pronounced; letting the spelling decide instead of the following letter's class produces an unused form
forbidden_answers: the article's lām is pronounced the same way before every letter
the written lām is always audible regardless of the following letter's class
sun-letter assimilation is optional in careful speech
required_reasoning: pronunciation of the lām tied to the class of the following letter
lām identified as orthographic only before a sun letter
lām identified as staying audible before a moon letter
